one_liner: Header-only C++14 JSON-to-BSON parser; author's 2015 runs: 1.46x faster than JsonCpp on canada.json, 9x slower than RapidJSON.
what_it_does: jbson builds and iterates BSON documents and parses JSON (UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32 ranges, plus a subset of MongoDB extended JSON) straight into a BSON byte buffer. The result is a basic_document or basic_array: a constant wrapper over a std::vector<char> (or any container or range) that you walk with iterators, element visitors and get<T>(), not a mutable DOM. Edits need a conversion to document_set (a std::set of elements), and a JSONPath evaluator, builder classes and _json_doc literals sit on top. It is not a drop-in for JsonCpp's Json::Value API.
how_it_is_fast: The reader reserves one std::vector<char> the size of the input and appends type bytes, names, length-prefixed strings and little-endian numbers into it in a single recursive-descent pass, so there is no per-node heap allocation, std::map or Value object as in JsonCpp. Numbers go through Boost.Spirit Qi's int and real parsers; integers that fit int32 are stored as 4 bytes. Reading is lazy: elements are decoded from the buffer only when iterated. Nothing is SIMD or table-driven, and every character passes through a Boost.Spirit line_pos_iterator that tracks line numbers for error messages, which is one reason it stays far behind RapidJSON.
when_to_use: You need JSON converted to BSON bytes (for example to hand to MongoDB-style storage or a BSON wire format) and want one header-only, BSL-licensed C++ library that does both.
Parse once, iterate sequentially: config or message documents that are walked front to back rather than randomly indexed.
Memory matters more than speed and the alternative is a node-per-value DOM such as JsonCpp: the author's sanSS runs show 24,708 K vs 44,224 K on medium objects.
Legacy code that already depends on Boost and a 2015-era libc++ toolchain, where the library is known to build.
when_not_to_use: Raw parse speed is the goal: by the author's own numbers RapidJSON parses canada.json about 9x faster (4.86 s vs 43.0 s per 1000 parses), and yyjson and simdjson are faster still.

Random access into large documents or arrays: find() is a linear scan, and array index lookup does std::to_string(idx) and then a linear name comparison, so indexed loops over a large array are quadratic.
Input you do not control: there is no fuzzing, and the literal, \u-escape and post-whitespace checks dereference the iterator without testing for end of input (see gotchas).

Strict JSON round-tripping: the BSON model cannot hold NUL in names, \u0000 is stored as the six characters \u0000, integers beyond int64 throw instead of becoming doubles, and number validation rejects valid 0e5 while accepting invalid -01.
Any maintained or modern-toolchain project: the last commit was 2015-12-20 and the headers depend on Library Fundamentals TS headers and std::wstring_convert.

integration.dependencies: Boost 1.55 or newer (headers only: Range, Spirit Qi, Exception, Predef, lexical_cast, ios_state); the optional test build fetches googletest r660 from googletest.googlecode.com SVN
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (-std=c++1y) with <codecvt>, <experimental/optional> and <experimental/string_view>; README says it is known to work only with an up-to-date (2015) libc++ and fails on gcc 4.8/4.9 libstdc++
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar C++); BSON numbers are written little-endian via native_to_little_endian
integration.thread_safety: not documented; json_reader keeps per-parse state, so use one reader per thread

gotchas: Extended-JSON handling is broken for everything except $oid: parse_extended_value compares basic_document::size(), which returns the BSON size in bytes (at least 5), against 1 or 2 for $date, $timestamp, $undefined, $minkey, $maxkey, $binary/$type, $regex/$options and $ref/$id, so any object whose first key is one of those always throws json_parse_error. This includes ordinary JSON such as JSON Schema subschemas of the form {"$ref": "#/definitions/x"}; the tests cover only $oid and a $binary case that is expected to throw.

Bounds checks are missing on malformed or truncated input: true/false/null are matched with std::next(first, 4 or 5) past the end, \u escapes read four characters without an end check, and parse_document/parse_array test *first for ':' , ',' or '}' right after skip_space without checking first == last. With std::string input this usually hits the terminating NUL; with other ranges it is an out-of-range read.

Number edge cases: integers outside int64 fail Spirit's extract_int and throw; 0e5 and 0E-3 (valid JSON) are rejected by the leading-zero check, while -01 (invalid JSON) is accepted; \u0000 is kept as the literal text \u0000.
Element names are always copied, and elements obtained from a document hold iterator ranges into its buffer, so they must not outlive the document unless copied into jbson::element (README).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick jbson over yyjson, simdjson or the C parsers Jansson and json-c only when BSON output itself is the requirement and a header-only Boost-based C++ library fits; for plain JSON parsing every one of those siblings is the better choice, and jsoncons (5.7x slower than jbson in the 2015 README) is catalogued separately with newer numbers.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran mloskot/json_benchmark (1000 parses of canada.json, 2,251,060 bytes) and reports jbson 43.0 s vs JsonCpp 62.8 s (1.46x), QJsonDocument 58.1 s (1.35x), jsoncons 243.6 s and RapidJSON 4.86 s, i.e. about 52 MB/s vs 36 MB/s for JsonCpp and 463 MB/s for RapidJSON (derived from page data), plus about 1.9x over JsonCpp on 500 small documents; sanSS json-bechmarks gives 64.8 ms vs 121.0 ms on medium objects. No compiler, flags, CPU or library versions are given, and the jbson adapter used in both suites is not published; the repo's own test/perf_test.cpp only self-times 1000 parses of a sample file with no baseline.
status_note: Abandoned since 2015-12-20 (261 commits, 38 stars, 2 open issues including an unimplemented binary element type, #7); BSL-1.0 and header-only so it can be vendored, but expect to patch it for a current compiler and standard library.
